sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
Barbell Shrugs Behind Back is a trapezius-building exercise performed by holding a barbell behind your body with an overhand grip and shrugging the shoulders upward.

The behind-the-back position emphasizes the upper and mid trapezius while also engaging the rear deltoids and rhomboids.

This variation, sometimes called Haney Shrugs after bodybuilder Lee Haney, is valued for building thickness and strength in the upper back and traps.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Targets upper and mid trapezius effectively
- Engages rear deltoids and rhomboids more than front shrugs
- Improves posture and shoulder stability
- Builds upper back thickness and width
- Strengthens grip and forearms
- Reduces forward shoulder roll compared to front shrugs
- Complements other pulling movements

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Upper Trapezius, Middle Trapezius

Secondary: Rear Deltoids, Rhomboids, Levator Scapulae, Forearms and Grip

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart.
2. Hold a barbell behind your back with an overhand grip.
3. Position your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart.
4. Let the bar rest against the back of your thighs or glutes.
5. Keep your back straight and chest lifted.
6. Relax your arms and shoulders.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Lift your shoulders as high as possible by shrugging them towards your ears.
2. Squeeze your trapezius at the top of the movement.
3. Lower your shoulders back down under control.
4. Repeat the shrug for the desired number of repetitions.
5. Focus on engaging your shoulder and upper back muscles.
6. Maintain proper posture throughout the movement.
7. Adjust the weight as needed.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Rolling the shoulders instead of shrugging straight up
- Using too much weight and compromising form
- Bending the arms to assist the lift
- Leaning forward or rounding the back
- Insufficient range of motion
- Jerking the weight with momentum
- Allowing the bar to drift away from the body
- Not pausing at the top to maximize contraction

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Olympic Barbell (45 lbs/20 kg)
- Weight Plates
- Optional: Lifting Straps (for grip assistance)
- Optional: Chalk (improves grip)
- Optional: Power Rack (for easier unracking)
- Flat-soled shoes recommended

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Stance: Feet shoulder-width apart.
2. Grip: Overhand, slightly wider than shoulders.
3. Bar Position: Behind back, resting against thighs/glutes.
4. Arms: Fully extended, relaxed.
5. Chest: Lifted, shoulders back.
6. Back: Straight with natural arch.
7. Head: Neutral, eyes forward.
8. Core: Engaged for stability.

sections.heading: Progression Tips
sections.content:
1. Start with light weight to master the movement.
2. Use a power rack to unrack the bar safely.
3. Focus on straight-up shrug motion.
4. Add pauses at the top for greater contraction.
5. Gradually increase weight as strength improves.
6. Use straps when grip becomes the limiting factor.
7. Keep reps in the 8-15 range for hypertrophy.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Barbell Shrugs (Front): Traditional variation with bar in front
- Dumbbell Shrug: Allows greater range of motion
- Trap Bar Shrug: Neutral grip, comfortable positioning
- Kettlebell Shrug: Alternative implement for shrug movement
- Cable Shrug: Constant tension variation
- Smith Machine Shrug: Fixed bar path for stability

sections.heading: Trap Variations
sections.content:
Barbell Shrug Front: Classic trap builder
Dumbbell Shrug: Free range of motion
Trap Bar Shrug: Neutral hand position
Cable Face Pull: Rear delt and upper trap combo
Farmer's Carry: Dynamic trap and grip work
Rack Pull Shrug: Heavy overload for traps

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Shoulder Impingement: Try dumbbell shrugs with neutral grip
Grip Issues: Use lifting straps
Lower Back Pain: Reduce weight, focus on form
Limited Mobility: Use a trap bar instead
No Barbell: Substitute dumbbells or kettlebells
Beginner: Start with lighter front shrugs first
